name: Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr.
subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
facts: Atty. Quirino P. Revilla, Jr., a notary public, notarized a complaint-affidavit signed by three people: Heneraline L. Brosas (the sister of his wife), Herizalyn Brosas Pedrosa (his wife's sister-in-law), and Elmer L. Alvarado (the live-in houseboy of the Brosas family). He did not ask any of them to show valid ID cards. Bernard N. Jandoquile filed a complaint asking the Supreme Court to disbar him. Atty. Revilla, Jr. admitted the facts. He argued that this single act is not a ground for disbarment, that he acted more as the three signers' lawyer than as a notary public, and that he did not need their IDs because he knows them personally.
issue: Should Atty. Revilla, Jr. be disbarred for (1) notarizing a complaint-affidavit signed by relatives of his wife, and (2) not asking the signers to show valid ID cards?
ruling: No disbarment, but he was penalized. (1) He violated the disqualification rule in Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, because two of the signers are his relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity (relatives through marriage). He should have refused to notarize. The Court rejected his claim that he acted as their lawyer and not as a notary public: the notarial certificate at the bottom of the document bore his signature as a notary public. (2) He was not liable for skipping the IDs. A notary public who knows the signers personally need not ask for their IDs, as shown by the definition of a jurat. But he was at fault for not stating in the jurat that he knows them personally. (3) His violation was not deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, gross immoral conduct, or any other serious ground for disbarment under Section 27, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court. Since disbarment should not be imposed when a lighter penalty will do, he was reprimanded and disqualified from being commissioned as a notary public, or from performing any notarial act, for three months. He was also told to inform the Court by affidavit once those three months are over.
keyDoctrine: A notary public may not notarize a document if the principal (the person whose act is being notarized) is a relative by affinity or consanguinity within the fourth civil degree, even if the notary is also that person's lawyer. A notary who personally knows the signers need not ask for their IDs, but should say in the jurat that they are personally known. A single violation like this is not a ground for disbarment; a lighter penalty is enough.

name: Zulueta v. Court of Appeals
subject: Communication Law
facts: Cecilia Zulueta is the wife of Dr. Alfredo Martin. On March 26, 1982, she entered her husband's medical clinic and, in the presence of her mother, a driver, and his secretary, forcibly opened the drawers and cabinet there. She took 157 documents and papers: private letters between Dr. Martin and his alleged mistresses, greeting cards, cancelled checks, diaries, his passport, and photographs. She wanted to use them as evidence in the case she had filed against him for legal separation and for disqualification from practicing medicine. Dr. Martin sued to get the papers back and for damages. The trial court ruled for him, ordered her to return the papers, made her pay damages, and barred her and her lawyers from using the papers as evidence. The Court of Appeals agreed. Zulueta's only argument before the Supreme Court was that in an earlier disbarment case against her lawyer (Martin v. Felix, Jr.), the Court had already ruled these papers admissible as evidence.
issue: Are the papers that the wife took from her husband's clinic, without his knowledge and consent, admissible as evidence, on the theory that the Court already held them admissible in the earlier disbarment case against her lawyer?
ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) The earlier case did not decide that the papers were admissible. The lawyer was cleared in that case only because, when he used the papers, the trial court's order banning their use was temporarily stopped by the Supreme Court's restraining order (TRO). Once that TRO was lifted, the ban applied again. (2) The papers are inadmissible. The Constitution says the privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable, and this applies even when the person who violated it is the wife. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. (3) Marriage does not take away a person's right to privacy. The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking into the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity. The law protects free communication between spouses by making it privileged, but freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share everything they know with the other.
keyDoctrine: The constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3) applies even between husband and wife. Evidence obtained in violation of it is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. A person does not give up their right to privacy by getting married.

name: Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr.
subject: Communication Law
facts: Spouses Bill and Victoria Hing own a lot in Mandaue City, Cebu. Next to it is a building of Aldo Development & Resources, Inc. (Aldo), where an auto-repair shop operates. Aldo had earlier sued the Hings, claiming their fence construction would destroy its wall, but that court denied Aldo's request for an injunction (a court order to stop an act) for lack of proof. The Hings then sued Alexander Choachuy, Sr. and Allan Choachuy. They said that, to gather evidence for Aldo's case, the Choachuys installed two video surveillance cameras on Aldo's building facing the Hings' property, and had employees take pictures of the Hings' construction without consent. The Choachuys said they did not install the cameras and were only stockholders of Aldo, not its owners. After an ocular inspection (the judge visited and viewed the site), the trial court ordered them to remove a revolving camera that viewed the Hings' lot and move it elsewhere. The Court of Appeals annulled that order. It reasoned that the Civil Code's protection of the privacy of one's residence did not apply because the property was not used as a residence, and that the Choachuys, as mere stockholders, could not have installed the cameras.
issue: (1) Did installing surveillance cameras facing the Hings' property violate their right to privacy, even though the property was not used as a residence? (2) Were the Choachuys the proper parties to be sued, even though Aldo, not they, owned the building?
ruling: The petition was granted and the trial court's injunction was reinstated. (1) Yes, there was a violation. The right to privacy is simply 'the right to be let alone.' Article 26(1) of the Civil Code forbids prying into the privacy of another's residence, but it also covers 'similar acts.' Following Tolentino, a business office is entitled to the same privacy when the public is excluded and only allowed persons may enter. So the protection covers places, locations, or even situations a person considers private, as long as society recognizes that right. Courts use the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, a two-part test: (a) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy; and (b) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. This is decided case by case. Surveillance cameras should not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy unless the affected person consents, and should not be used to pry into another's residence or business office, which would be no different from eavesdropping, a crime under R.A. No. 4200 (Anti-Wiretapping Law). The Hings had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their property, whether used as a business office or residence, so cameras facing it or covering a significant part of it without their consent clearly violated their privacy. (2) Yes, the Choachuys were proper parties. Not owning the building does not mean they did not cause the cameras to be installed. Aldo is a family corporation managed by the Choachuy family, there was a long-running boundary dispute between the two families, and the Choachuys let the court inspect the building and argued that Aldo would be damaged if the cameras were moved. They were using Aldo's separate corporate personality as a shield.
keyDoctrine: The right to privacy under Article 26(1) of the Civil Code is not limited to a residence. It extends to places where a person has the right to exclude the public, like a business office. Whether privacy was violated is decided by the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test: (1) did the person, by their conduct, show an expectation of privacy, and (2) is that expectation one society recognizes as reasonable. Surveillance cameras may not cover places where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy without the affected person's consent.

name: Vivares v. St. Theresa's College
subject: Communication Law
facts: Julia and Julienne, both minors, were graduating high school students at St. Theresa's College (STC) in Cebu City. In January 2012, while changing into swimsuits for a beach party, they and others took pictures of themselves in their undergarments. Another student, Angela, uploaded the pictures to her Facebook profile. Escudero, an STC computer teacher, learned about the photos from her students. Using STC's computers, those students logged into their own Facebook accounts and showed her more photos of the girls, including photos of them drinking and smoking in a bar and walking the streets in clothes that showed their brassieres. The students said that at times these photos were viewable by any Facebook user. Escudero reported this to STC's discipline officer. STC found that the girls broke the Student Handbook and barred them from the graduation ceremony. Julia's mother (Vivares) and Julienne's parents (the Suzaras) then filed a petition for a writ of habeas data (a court remedy to protect a person's information privacy). They said the girls' Facebook accounts were set to 'Friends Only,' that Escudero intruded into the accounts and saved and showed the photos without consent, and that STC spread them by attaching them to its court papers in a related case. The trial court dismissed the petition.
issue: Should a writ of habeas data be issued? More specifically, was there an actual or threatened violation of the minors' right to privacy when STC viewed and used the Facebook photos?
ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) Procedural points: The writ of habeas data is not limited to cases of extralegal killings and enforced disappearances. It is an independent remedy to enforce the right to informational privacy. Also, the person or entity sued need not be in the business of gathering data. To be 'engaged' in gathering, collecting, or storing data just means doing or taking part in it. (2) The right to informational privacy is the right of individuals to control information about themselves. Having an expectation of privacy is not incompatible with using online social networks (OSNs) like Facebook. But a user must first show the intention to keep a post private by using the OSN's privacy tools. Using these tools is how a person claims informational privacy online. (3) Here, the girls did not prove they limited who could see the photos. Their claim that only five people could see them was self-serving. They did not dispute that the girls' Facebook friends showed the photos using their own accounts, with no special means. Since Facebook's default setting is 'Public,' the photos may be presumed viewable by everyone. Even a 'Friends Only' setting does not make a post very private, because friends can share posts or tag others, which widens the audience. STC officials were mere recipients of photos voluntarily shown by people who had legitimate access to them. They used no unlawful means, and attaching the photos to court papers was not a privacy violation. The result might have been different if the photos had been set to 'Only Me' or a 'Custom' list. (4) On cyber responsibility: internet users must be careful and use privacy tools if they want to keep information private. The Court cannot protect people who did nothing to put the matter within their private zone.
keyDoctrine: The right to informational privacy is the right to control information about oneself. A social media user has a reasonable expectation of privacy only if they show the intention to keep a post private by using the platform's privacy tools to limit who can see it. A 'Public' or even 'Friends Only' post is not automatically private. A writ of habeas data needs proof, at least by substantial evidence, of an actual or threatened violation of the right to privacy in life, liberty, or security. It is not limited to extralegal killings and enforced disappearances.
